name: Suryanar Koil (Sun Temple)
deity: Suryanar, the Sun God, worshipped as the presiding deity with his consorts Ushadevi and Chhayadevi (Pratyusha Devi); each of the nine planets has a separate shrine facing him.

location.city: Suryanar Koil, near Aduthurai and Kumbakonam

period: Chola period, associated with Kulottunga Chola I
dynasty: Chola, with later Nayak and Maratha additions
summary: The principal Navagraha temple and the only major South Indian shrine where Surya himself presides. Here all nine planets stand in their own sanctums, turned toward the Sun, and pilgrims resolve every planetary affliction in one visit.

sections.history: Suryanar Koil rose in the Chola era and is traditionally linked to Kulottunga Chola I, whose reign bridged the eleventh and twelfth centuries. From its beginnings it was conceived not as an ordinary shrine but as the head of the nine Navagraha Sthalams that dot the Kaveri delta around Kumbakonam, a distinction it still carries. Over the centuries rulers who followed the Cholas, including the Nayaks and later the Marathas, extended its halls and enclosures, leaving a temple whose fabric records successive devotions. It remains a living centre of planetary worship, drawing pilgrims who come to honour the Sun as a god one can address directly.
sections.architecture: Built in the Dravidian idiom, the temple is unusual in its very plan: Surya presides in the central sanctum while each of the nine planets, the Navagraha, is given a shrine of its own, all arranged so that the grahas face the Sun. This layout, rare among South Indian temples where the Navagraha usually share a single platform, makes the architecture itself an expression of the temple's theology. Pillared halls, a gopuram, and enclosures added by later dynasties frame the sanctums, while the eastward orientation of the principal shrine lets the morning sun fall toward the deity it honours.
sections.legends: The temple's tradition tells of sages and of the planets themselves worshipping Shiva at this spot. Through that devotion the nine grahas are said to have received their power to shape the fortunes of living beings, becoming lords of destiny under the divine order. Because all nine were sanctified together here, devotees believe that the doshas, the afflictions attributed to unfavourable planetary positions, can be eased at a single place rather than at nine scattered shrines. Pilgrims accordingly come to Suryanar Koil to make peace with every planet at once, offering prayers for relief and for the turning of adverse periods.
sections.festivals: Ratha Saptami, the day sacred to the Sun's northward course, is the temple's foremost occasion, when special abhishekams honour Suryanar. Days held sacred to each of the nine grahas also draw worshippers seeking that planet's grace, and periodic Surya-related observances swell the crowds. Throughout the year the grahas receive ritual bathing and offerings of lamps, and on festival days the temple stays open longer to accommodate the pilgrims who gather for the abhishekams and the lighting of lamps before each planetary shrine.
sections.experience: A visit to Suryanar Koil has a rhythm unlike other temples: worshippers move from shrine to shrine, greeting each planet in turn as they might greet a presiding elder, before returning to the Sun at the centre. The air carries camphor, the murmur of planetary hymns, and the soft clink of lamp offerings. Many arrive with a specific concern about a difficult period in life, and the practice of addressing all nine grahas in one enclosure lends the visit a sense of completeness. Come in the cool of early morning, when the eastern light reaches the sanctum, for the most fitting darshan of a god of light.

visit.timings: Generally open around 6:00 am to 1:00 pm and 4:00 pm to 8:30 pm; hours are extended on festival days. Timings can change, so verify locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected. Cover the shoulders and legs; footwear is removed before entering the temple.
visit.photography: Photography inside the sanctum is generally not permitted. Observe posted signs and the instructions of temple staff, and ask before photographing elsewhere.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in Suryanar Koil village near Aduthurai, about 15 km from Kumbakonam in Thanjavur district. Kumbakonam is the nearest hub, with rail access via Aduthurai or Kumbakonam; the nearest airport is Tiruchirappalli, roughly 90 km away. Buses and taxis run from Kumbakonam.
